supplement.where: Appendices A to D are included in this PDF (pp. 13-27). The project data, analysis code, and interactive dashboard are linked at https://ainewsaudit.github.io/ (p. 1 header; p. 2, Contributions and footnotes 3-4). The release contains article links and metadata, not full texts (p. 2, footnote 3; p. 10, Ethical Considerations). No separate supplement or code-repository URL is stated.
supplement.holds: A: collection details, topic prompt and definitions, circulation and ownership sources (Figures 5-7, Tables 4-5, pp. 13-16). B: how Pangram's fine-grained labels are combined into three, and the GPTZero comparison (p. 16). C and D.3: the ai_reporters dataset (Figure 8, Table 6, Table 13, Figures 20-24, pp. 16-27). D.1: more recent_news results, including the newspaper-level circulation test, hallucination audit, quote-level detection, duplicate clusters, machine-translation test (Table 10), and topic-bias test (pp. 17-22). D.2: opinions label distribution, Table 11, and the op-ed examples in Table 12 (pp. 22-24). No creativity or diversity statistics.

paper_design_summary: The authors analyzed three corpora of published U.S. newspaper articles with the Pangram v2 AI-text detector: 186,507 articles from 1,528 newspapers (June 15 to September 15, 2025), 44,803 opinion pieces from the NYT, WaPo, and WSJ (August 2022 to September 2025), and 20,132 articles by 10 reporters selected for detected AI use (2011 to 2025) (p. 3, Sections 2.1-2.3 and Table 1; p. 16, Appendix C; p. 17, Figure 8). They report the share of articles labeled AI-generated or mixed by circulation, topic, ownership, language, outlet, and year, plus manual audits of disclosure and hallucinations. No person is assigned to AI, and no creativity, novelty, or diversity outcome is scored.

eligibility.reason: This is a corpus audit of detected AI text in published U.S. newspaper articles. The corpora were collected after publication and labeled by Pangram; people were not assigned to AI assistance (p. 3, Sections 2.1-2.3; p. 16, Appendix C). There is no participant sample in an AI-assistance study: article and corpus-author counts do not establish an analyzed sample of at least 50 participants (p. 3, Table 1; p. 16, Appendix C). The analyses concern AI-text prevalence, disclosure, factuality, and detector robustness, with no scored creativity or diversity outcome (pp. 3-9, Sections 2-6; pp. 16-27, Appendices B-D). Cosine similarity identifies republished-article clusters whose AI-label rates are counted; it does not measure an AI-related change in diversity across different writers (p. 20, Appendix D.1, Effects of republishing articles). The em-dash and specificity discussion supplies stylistic observations, not a creativity or diversity score (p. 17, Appendix C; p. 18, Table 6). Under the codebook, AI-text prevalence studies without a diversity outcome are excluded from both the core dataset and observational context.

one_line_finding: Pangram labels 9.1 percent of 186,507 recent U.S. newspaper articles as AI-generated (5.2 percent) or mixed (3.9 percent) (p. 4, Section 3.1) and flags NYT, WaPo, and WSJ opinion pieces 6.4 times as often as the same outlets' news articles (4.56 vs. 0.71 percent; p. 8 and Table 11, p. 23); a manual audit finds that 96.5 percent of authors of 200 AI-flagged articles did not disclose AI use (p. 6), and the paper scores no creativity or diversity outcome.
notes: Out of scope for the creativity section: the paper measures how often published journalism contains detected AI text and whether that use is disclosed. No outcome bears on with_ai, across_people, or after_ai, so every outcomes list is empty. Analyses not coded as outcomes: AI-use share by circulation, state, topic, ownership, language, outlet, and year (Figures 1-4, 8-15, 18-24; Tables 1, 11, 13); disclosure audit of 200 AI-flagged articles (96.5 percent of authors and 94.0 percent of publishers did not disclose; p. 6, footnote 23); hallucination audit of 100 AI-GENERATED vs. 100 HUMAN-WRITTEN articles (41 vs. 5 percent; p. 7 and pp. 18-19); quote-level detection (pp. 19-20); AI labels among duplicate clusters formed by cosine similarity of 0.85 or more (6.7 percent of all duplicates, 3.1 percent of exact duplicates, 14.3 percent of semantically similar ones; p. 20); machine-translation test (Table 10, p. 22); topic-bias test (pp. 21-22). Overlap is within the paper only: ai_reporters is drawn from recent_news, and Table 11's news articles come from recent_news (p. 8, footnote 29). The finalizer read the entire markdown conversion, including Appendices A-D through Figure 24, and independently checked the eligibility evidence and recorded numbers against the PDF. The earlier note that the markdown stopped at Appendix B was incorrect. Internal inconsistencies in the paper, none of which affects screening: Table 1 (p. 3) prints MIXED 3.98 percent while Section 3.1 (p. 4) and Appendix D.1 (p. 17) print 3.9 percent; Appendix A (p. 14) counts 1,560 unique newspapers against 1,528 in Table 1 (p. 3); Table 7 (p. 18) totals 186,512 articles against 186,507 in Table 1 (p. 3). The candidate record's library labels ('Corpus', theme 'Academic & scientific writing') do not match the document, which studies newspapers. Screener B's S2 assignment quote dropped a comma; this form uses the verbatim text. No c020 challenge files were present. There were no open questions or unresolved reconciliation differences to carry forward; the final challenge counts are therefore zero. Provenance wording and the eligibility explanation were clarified independently of challenges.
